ON-DEMAND - Too Many Findings, Not Enough Meaning: Building an AWS-Native Security Graph for Permission Governance, Boundary Detection, and Threat Containment

AVAILABLE 17 DECEMBER IN THE MOBILE APPON-DEMAND ONLY
Chandler Niu |  Security Researcher, Bitget Security Lab
Jesse Cao |  Security Expert, Bitget Security Lab
Aaron |  Security Director, Bitget Security Lab
Date: 10 Dec 2026 | 22:30-23:00 ( On-Demand )
Format: 30-Minute Briefings
Tracks:
Defense & Resilience,
Cloud Security
Vault Recording: TBD

Your AWS environment changed again overnight. IAM roles gained or retained access to thousands of resources, test accounts acquired new network paths into protected workloads, Inspector reported vulnerable assets, and GuardDuty raised suspicious-activity findings. Which of these signals represents real business risk—and which Security Group, IAM permission, or AWS relationship should defenders change first?

Most cloud security tools answer only one part of that question. Static IAM analysis shows what a role can do, but not how those permissions are used on each connected resource. CloudTrail shows observed activity, but not whether an unusual permission reaches a critical business asset. Raw graph diff reports every changed edge, but not whether hundreds of edges represent one boundary failure. Inspector and GuardDuty identify local asset risk, but do not explain the downstream network, identity, and business impact.

In this Briefing, we will show how we built an AWS-native security graph that combines network reachability, IAM permissions, CloudTrail behavior, AWS-native security findings, business context, and root-cause evidence. In a recent enterprise snapshot, the graph contained 61,330 active nodes and more than 5.9 million security-relevant relationships, including 4.32 million network edges and 1.61 million permission edges.

We will present two relationship-level permission analyses using 30 days of CloudTrail activity for 238 IAM roles associated with business-critical assets. The first compares configured and observed actions for each role-to-resource relationship to identify least-privilege review candidates. The second derives dominant permission patterns across groups of similar adjacent resources and identifies individual configuration outliers. The resulting report surfaced findings for 97 roles. Permission-convergence analysis compressed 37,483 adjacent relationships into 137 reviewable findings, while peer analysis identified isolated exceptions inside resource groups containing as many as 3,761 neighbors. Unobserved actions are treated as evidence for review—not as instructions for automatic removal.

We will also show how risk-adaptive aggregation converts network change into operational boundary events. In one cross-snapshot analysis, the system identified 1,670 newly added test-to-non-test network edges. Rather than generating 1,670 alerts, it preserved the edges as evidence and compressed them into 29 events: 28 destination-centric alerts involving business-critical assets or protected VPCs, and one account-pair summary. In one case, 92 new edges from two test accounts converged on a single critical EC2 workload and became one actionable alert tied to the Security Groups responsible for the access.

Finally, we will explain how the graph incorporates AWS-native exposure features, Inspector vulnerability evidence, and GuardDuty threat evidence to create explainable risk states. Inspector tells us what may be exploitable. GuardDuty tells us what may already be happening. The graph tells us what the affected asset can reach, why it matters to the business, and which AWS control can contain it.

Attendees will leave with practical algorithms and design patterns for turning millions of AWS relationships into a small number of explainable permission findings, business-boundary events, and defensive decisions.

Briefing is available On-Demand only to Briefings Pass Holders via the Black Hat Events App, December 17 - January 29.

Takeaway

  • A practical method for building an AWS-native security graph that combines network reachability, IAM permissions, CloudTrail behavior, Inspector and GuardDuty findings, business-critical asset context, and remediable AWS root-cause evidence.
  • Relationship-level techniques for comparing configured and observed IAM actions, finding permission outliers among thousands of similar adjacent resources, and converting the results into reviewable least-privilege governance candidates rather than unsafe automatic removals.
  • A risk-adaptive approach for preserving large volumes of graph evidence while compressing them into business-relevant events, tracing those events to Security Groups and IAM configurations, and using AWS-native threat and vulnerability evidence to prioritize containment.

Below the Model: Least-Privilege Containment for Autonomous Browser Agents in Chromium

Ariel Koren |  Innovation
Elad Mintzer |  Innovation
Shlomi Azoulay |  Machine Learning Engineer and Security Researcher,  
Date: 9 Dec 2026 | 10:20-11:00 ( Victoria 4, Level 3 )
Format: 40-Minute Briefings
Tracks:
Application Security: Defense,
AI & ML: Attack and Defense
Vault Recording: TBD

An agent shopping for earbuds reads a product review that tells it to add a protection plan first. It obeys, and the cart lands 34 percent over the user's hard cap. Nothing malfunctioned. A language model cannot reliably separate the user's instructions from attacker-controlled page text, because both arrive as tokens inside the same reasoning context. Once the model is hijacked, the browser still gives the agent the user's full authority.

This research takes the opposite route from model-side hardening. Instead of asking the model to behave, it moves enforcement below the model and into Chromium. Every browser-driving agent ultimately speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol, so the browser turns that dispatch point into a deterministic least-privilege chokepoint. Each automation client receives a transport-derived identity the model cannot spoof. Hundreds of protocol commands collapse into a small set of semantic action types. Every action receives an allow, block, or native human-confirmation verdict.

The agent also declares, per subtask, which origins and action classes it needs. The browser enforces the intersection between that declaration and the baseline policy. A declaration can only narrow authority, never widen it. Off-scope origins receive an empty ephemeral cookie jar through partial-incognito routing, so a shopping task cannot read the user's inbox or steal unrelated session credentials. The Briefing demonstrates three live browser-agent hijacks, then shows each one contained by browser-side enforcement. The model reasons. The browser decides.

Takeaway

  • A practical architecture for placing the AI-agent security boundary below the model. The Chrome DevTools Protocol dispatch point becomes a least-privilege chokepoint that a compromised agent cannot route around, while client identity is derived from transport state rather than model text.
  • A threat model for browser-agent hijack as runtime drift. The Briefing separates four concrete drift classes discovered through live attacks: context drift, origin drift, cookie-session drift, and budget drift. Each class maps to a browser-side enforcement point that teams can test against their own agents.
  • A deployable credential-isolation primitive for agentic browsing: partial incognito. In-scope origins receive the user's real cookies, autofill, and permissions. Off-scope origins receive an empty ephemeral jar inside the same browsing task. There is no URL blocklist to maintain, and unrelated session credentials are not exposed to the agent.

Native binary editing is missing one of its basic atomic primitives: local insertion. Modern reverse engineering tools make it easy to overwrite existing instructions, but inserting bytes inside an already compiled executable while preserving its semantics remains unsupported in practice.

Insertion is not just a larger patch. Replacement preserves layout; insertion changes it. Once bytes are inserted inside .text, nearby code moves while the binary's embedded assumptions about addresses and metadata remain tied to the old layout. Relative control-flow displacements, RIP-relative references, relocation-backed pointers, exception metadata, jump tables, security metadata, and compiler-generated structures may all need to stay synchronized. Missing even one hidden reference can cause silent corruption, delayed crashes, or broken control flow.

The broader impact is two-sided: for reverse engineers, red teams, and instrumentation developers, local insertion enables modifications that previously required trampolines, code caves, or new sections; for defenders and malware analysts, it challenges PE tampering assumptions built around those structural artifacts. The takeaway is that in-place insertion is not merely another patching trick, but a missing primitive with practical consequences for both binary modification and detection.

Package Manager records the component at installation, but a later system-service lifecycle becomes the parser of the package-owned bytes.

Our first proof used this separation to inject an enormous UTF-16 value through Account Manager. The crash was reproduced but rejected as a security issue because Safe Mode could remove the third-party package. That rejection changed the research question: does Safe Mode actually prevent every privileged lifecycle from resolving attacker-controlled resources? It does not.

We found direct Package Manager lookups that bypass Safe Mode's intent-resolution filter (C1), boot-time metadata queries that execute before the filter becomes active (C2), and a Device Admin revocation deadlock in which the only removal UI parses resources owned by the admin it must remove. We also reconstructed a complementary remote path: a crafted DNG received by the preinstalled messaging application is rendered by SystemUI as notification content, replayed after SystemUI restarts, and rebuilt from persistent message state after reboot. Safe Mode keeps both privileged components enabled, so a trusted package identity continues to replay attacker-controlled media.

Framework-realistic fuzzing supplied the XML, drawable, and native-image failure primitives used to exercise these recovery paths. We use recovery-resistant PDoS to mean that ordinary reboot, Safe Mode, and normal role-removal or uninstall flows do not restore a usable device. Factory reset remains effective, and privileged ADB or recovery intervention may also recover a suitably configured device.

The campaign produced 33 tracked reports, 12 rated Critical and 15 rated High, which were assigned 18 Android CVEs.

The Linux boot chain is built on a layered trust model where each component - from UEFI firmware through Shim, GRUB, and the kernel - verifies the next before passing control. Secure Boot, measured boot, and signature enforcement are designed to ensure that only authorized code executes before the operating system starts. However, the security of this model depends entirely on the integrity of every stage, and weaknesses at any point can subvert the entire trust foundation.

While UEFI bootkits targeting Windows have been publicly documented and studied for years, the Linux boot chain has received significantly less attention from an offensive research perspective. Despite recent indicators that firmware-level threats against Linux are emerging, there is still no complete, publicly available UEFI bootkit implementation that can be studied and reproduced end to end.

This Briefing presents a fully functional UEFI bootkit for Linux capable of hooking and modifying every stage of the boot chain in memory, from Shim through GRUB to the compressed kernel, enabling unsigned kernel code to execute on fully updated systems with Secure Boot enabled. We walk through the complete infection chain, demonstrating how each trust boundary is identified, targeted, and subverted through specific hooking and patching techniques at the firmware level.

The Briefing covers the reverse engineering process required to understand the internal structures of each boot component, the specific techniques used to intercept and modify execution flow at each stage, how kernel integrity mechanisms are bypassed before the operating system initializes, and how the bootkit enables the deployment of kernel-level rootkits for post-compromise persistence. All source code, reverse engineering notes, and multiple Linux kernel rootkits will be publicly released, providing the security community with a complete framework to study, reproduce, and defend against firmware-level threats targeting Linux.

Most cloud security tools answer only one part of that question. Static IAM analysis shows what a role can do, but not how those permissions are used on each connected resource. CloudTrail shows observed activity, but not whether an unusual permission reaches a critical business asset. Raw graph diff reports every changed edge, but not whether hundreds of edges represent one boundary failure. Inspector and GuardDuty identify local asset risk, but do not explain the downstream network, identity, and business impact.

We will present two relationship-level permission analyses using 30 days of CloudTrail activity for 238 IAM roles associated with business-critical assets. The first compares configured and observed actions for each role-to-resource relationship to identify least-privilege review candidates. The second derives dominant permission patterns across groups of similar adjacent resources and identifies individual configuration outliers. The resulting report surfaced findings for 97 roles. Permission-convergence analysis compressed 37,483 adjacent relationships into 137 reviewable findings, while peer analysis identified isolated exceptions inside resource groups containing as many as 3,761 neighbors. Unobserved actions are treated as evidence for review—not as instructions for automatic removal.
